To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the adaptive chirplet and EMD methods can effectively capture the time-varying frequency content of non-stationary seismic signals and that they can be used to trace the evolution of the mean instantaneous frequencies of the response time-histories of a structure during the course of a seismic event.

the adaptive chirplet transform combined with the W-VDFT and the empirical mode decompositions combined with the Hilber transform are effective in capturing the temporal evolution in the frequency content of strong ground motions and structural response records.

(a) the adaptive chirplet transform combined with the WTC is an effective tool in the time–frequency domain representation of seismic signals; (b) the empirical mode decomposition is a very effective method in time–frequency domain analysis of seismic records; (c) both methods are capable of tracing the mean instantaneous frequencies of critical structural responses; and (d) the adaptive chirplets are more suitable in representing the frequency content of the signals in the time domain than the empirical mode decomposition.

the development of a methodology for the time–frequency analysis of earthquake ground motions and structural response records.
the development of a methodology that is capable of capturing and quantifying the time–frequency characteristics of the response of a structure to strong ground motion.
the development of an efficient methodology to extract the time-varying frequency content of non-stationary time histories.
